overview: Māori communities maintained distinct iwi and hapū histories through trade, technological change and colonisation. This card follows named examples of food production, fishing, carving and language education. The imported map endpoints do not mark an end to Māori society.

periods.title: Regional communities and authority
periods.summary: Local groups sustained relationships through whakapapa, mana, tapu and exchange. Shared cultural traditions existed alongside distinct authority and local histories.

periods.title: Food production in Waikato
periods.summary: At Tamahere, ancestors dated to this broad period had diets strongly based on plants. The result illuminates an inland community within a wider landscape of intensive gardening.

periods.title: Te Tiriti and differing expectations
periods.summary: The Māori and English texts of the Treaty describe authority differently. Kāwanatanga in Article 1 sits alongside the guarantee of tino rangatiratanga in Article 2 of the Māori text. These distinctions shaped expectations of the relationship with the Crown.

periods.title: Colonial dispossession and continuing communities
periods.summary: The New Zealand Settlements Act enabled extensive confiscation of Māori land. Losses also affected communities that had been neutral or aligned with the government. These events transformed access to land and livelihoods.

periods.title: Language transmission through whānau
periods.summary: The kōhanga reo movement developed immersion environments for children, with whānau responsible for management and cultural transmission.

items.text: A study of seven ancestors from Tamahere site S14/487, dated about 1700 to 1780, found diets predominantly based on plants. Archaeological context supports cultivated root crops as important foods. Isotopes do not identify each meal, and this small sample cannot describe all Māori diets.

The teeth of two children in the Tamahere study preserve a changing dietary signal consistent with weaning onto plant foods within their first two to three years. This is a finding about those children, not a universal rule for childhood across iwi.

sections.title: Fishing and the meaning of clothing

items.text: Te Papa’s pā kahawai lure OL000106/10, dated broadly to 1750 to 1850, combines a shaped and polished pāua-shell shank with a shell barb and tightly bound muka fibre. Fine notches decorate the shell. It preserves several stages of skilled manufacture in one small fishing implement.

Kākahu provided warmth and protection, while particular cloaks also expressed status and relationships. Their continued use as esteemed gifts and at funerals connects material workmanship with honour, care and ancestral memory. Everyday use and ceremonial importance should not be treated as interchangeable.

sections.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal

items.text: In the early 1840s, carvers led by Raharuhi Rukupo created Te Hau ki Tūranga at Orakaiapu pā, Manutuke. The whare whakairo belongs to Ngāti Kaipōhō of Rongowhakaata. Its carved ancestors and memorial purpose joined artistic work to hapū history and relationships.

In 1867 Crown troops dismantled Te Hau ki Tūranga and removed it despite objections. Rukupo recorded that he had refused requests to give it up. This documented removal is part of the building’s history alongside its artistry.

The Rongowhakaata settlement deed signed in 2011 acknowledges the wrongful taking of Te Hau ki Tūranga and records the Crown’s apology. The account recognises the harm caused by separating the taonga from its community.

The Treaty signed in 1840 survives in texts with different meanings. The Māori text speaks of kāwanatanga in Article 1 and guarantees tino rangatiratanga over lands, villages and taonga in Article 2; the English text uses sovereignty. Treating these as identical obscures the historical disagreement.

The New Zealand Settlements Act of 1863 enabled land confiscation from communities labelled rebellious. Confiscation also took land from Māori who had remained neutral or supported the government. The effects differed by region, with severe losses in Waikato and Taranaki.

For many iwi, Matariki connects seasonal knowledge with remembrance and sharing the harvest. Communities observe it in different ways and at different times. Its significance joins practical attention to the year with relationships among the living and the dead.

Pukeatua kōhanga reo opened in Wainuiomata in April 1982. The movement places children in Māori-language immersion environments and gives whānau responsibility for running centres. Education here includes language, relationships and cultural knowledge transmitted through daily life.

ending.text: Māori have no cultural fall date. Colonial war and confiscation transformed landholding and political authority, while communities persisted. Te Tiriti remains central to the history of their relationship with the Crown. Kōhanga reo exemplifies continuing whānau-led work to pass language and knowledge to future generations.
